La anciana tocó la campanilla y, en cuanto trajeron el servicio, procedió a distribuir rápidamente tazas y cucharas.
I and Adele went to the table; but the master did not leave his couch.
Adèle se sentó a la mesa, pero Rochester no abandonó su lugar.
"Will you hand Mr. Rochester's cup?" said Mrs. Fairfax to me; "Adele might perhaps spill it."
-¿Quiere usted alcanzar la taza al señor? -me preguntó Mrs. Fairfax-.
I did as requested.
Hice lo que me pedía.
As he took the cup from my hand, Adele, thinking the moment propitious for making a request in my favour, cried out--
Cuando él cogió la taza, Adèle, juzgando sin duda oportuno el momento para intervenir en mi favor, exclamó:
"N'est-ce pas, monsieur, qu'il y a un cadeau pour Mademoiselle Eyre dans votre petit coffre?"
-¿Verdad, señor, que hay un regalo para Miss Eyre en esa cajita?
"Who talks of cadeaux?" said he gruffly.
-¿Qué dices? -gruñó él-.
"Did you expect a present, Miss Eyre?
¿Esperaba usted algún regalo, Miss Eyre?
Are you fond of presents?" and he searched my face with eyes that I saw were dark, irate, and piercing.
¿Le gustan los regalos? Y me contempló con sus ojos duros y penetrantes.
"I hardly know, sir; I have little experience of them: they are generally thought pleasant things."
Tengo poca costumbre de recibirlos. La opinión general es que son cosas agradables.
"Generally thought?
-Yo no hablo de la opinión general.
But what do _you_ think?"
Digo si le gustan a usted.

"I should be obliged to take time, sir, before I could give you an answer worthy of your acceptance: a present has many faces to it, has it not? and one should consider all, before pronouncing an opinion as to its nature."
-Hay que pensarlo antes de contestar, señor. Aceptar un regalo puede ser tomado en muchos sentidos, y han de considerarse todos antes de opinar.
"Miss Eyre, you are not so unsophisticated as Adele: she demands a 'cadeau,' clamorously, the moment she sees me: you beat about the bush."
-Veo que es usted menos sencilla que Adèle. Ella, en cuanto me ve, me pide un regalo a gritos, mientras que usted, en cambio, filosofa sobre el asunto.

"Because I have less confidence in my deserts than Adele has: she can prefer the claim of old acquaintance, and the right too of custom; for she says you have always been in the habit of giving her playthings; but if I had to make out a case I should be puzzled, since I am a stranger, and have done nothing to entitle me to an acknowledgment."
-Porque yo tengo con usted menos confianza que Adèle. Ella está acostumbrada a que usted le compre juguetes, pero yo soy una extraña para usted y no tengo el mismo derecho.
"Oh, don't fall back on over-modesty!
-Déjese de modestias.
I have examined Adele, and find you have taken great pains with her: she is not bright, she has no talents; yet in a short time she has made much improvement."
He examinado a Adèle y he comprendido que se ha preocupado usted mucho de ella, porque la niña no tiene gran talento y, sin embargo, en poco tiempo ha progresado mucho.
"Sir, you have now given me my 'cadeau;' I am obliged to you: it is the meed teachers most covet--praise of their pupils' progress."
-Ya me ha dado usted mi regalo, señor. Para una maestra nada hay más halagador que oír elogiar los progresos de su discípula.
"Humph!" said Mr. Rochester, and he took his tea in silence.
-¡Hum! -murmuró Rochester. Y bebió su té en silencio.

"Come to the fire," said the master, when the tray was taken away, and Mrs. Fairfax had settled into a corner with her knitting; while Adele was leading me by the hand round the room, showing me the beautiful books and ornaments on the consoles and chiffonnieres.

-Acérquese al fuego-dijo después, mientras el ama de llaves se sentaba en un rincón a hacer calceta. Adèle me había cogido de la mano y me hacía girar por la estancia, mostrándome las consolas y cuanto había digno de verse.
We obeyed, as in duty bound; Adele wanted to take a seat on my knee, but she was ordered to amuse herself with Pilot.
Al oírle, le obedecimos. Adèle pretendió sentarse en mis rodillas, pero se le ordenó que fuese a jugar con Piloto.
"You have been resident in my house three months?"
-¿Vive usted en mi casa hace tres meses?
"Yes, sir."
-Sí, señor. -¿De dónde vino usted?
"And you came from--?" "From Lowood school, in ---shire."
-Del colegio de Lowood, en el condado de... -¡Ah, sí!
"Ah! a charitable concern.
Una institución benéfica.
How long were you there?"
¿Cuánto tiempo ha pasado usted allí?
"Eight years."
-Ocho años.
"Eight years! you must be tenacious of life. I thought half the time in such a place would have done up any constitution!
-¡Debe usted ser persona de mucho aguante para haber soportado ocho años de esa vida!
No wonder you have rather the look of another world. I marvelled where you had got that sort of face.
No me extraña que tenga usted la mirada de un ser del otro mundo.
When you came on me in Hay Lane last night, I thought unaccountably of fairy tales, and had half a mind to demand whether you had bewitched my horse: I am not sure yet.
Cuando la encontré anoche en el camino me pareció uno de esos seres fantásticos que figuran en los cuentos y temí que me hubiera embrujado el caballo. Aún no estoy seguro de lo contrario...
Who are your parents?"
¿Tiene usted padres?
"I have none." "Nor ever had, I suppose: do you remember them?" "No."
-No. -¿Ni se acuerda de ellos? -No.
"I thought not.
-Ya me lo figuraba.
And so you were waiting for your people when you sat on that stile?"
¿Y a quién esperaba usted sentada en el borde del camino? ¿A su gente?
"For whom, sir?"
-¿Cómo?
"For the men in green: it was a proper moonlight evening for them.
-Quiero decir si esperaba a los enanos del bosque.
Did I break through one of your rings, that you spread that damned ice on the causeway?"
Se me figura que, como castigo a haber roto uno de sus círculos mágicos, puso usted en el camino aquel condenado hielo.
I shook my head. "The men in green all forsook England a hundred years ago," said I, speaking as seriously as he had done.
Moví la cabeza. -Los enanos del bosque -dije hablando con tanta seriedad aparente como él- abandonaron Inglaterra hace más de cien años.
"And not even in Hay Lane, or the fields about it, could you find a trace of them.
Y ni siquiera en el camino de Hay ni en los campos próximos he podido encontrar rastros de ninguno.
I don't think either summer or harvest, or winter moon, will ever shine on their revels more."
Nunca volverán a danzar en las noches de verano ni bajo la fría luna de invierno...
Mrs. Fairfax had dropped her knitting, and, with raised eyebrows, seemed wondering what sort of talk this was.
Mrs. Fairfax, arqueando las cejas, mostró el asombro que le producía tan extravagante conversación.
"Well," resumed Mr. Rochester, "if you disown parents, you must have some sort of kinsfolk: uncles and aunts?"
Rochester-. Supongo que al menos tendrá usted tíos o tías.
"No; none that I ever saw." "And your home?" "I have none."
-Nunca los he visto. -¿Ni en su casa? -No tengo casa.
"Where do your brothers and sisters live?" "I have no brothers or sisters."
-¿Y sus hermanos? -No tengo hermanos.
"Who recommended you to come here?"
-¿Quién la recomendó aquí?
"I advertised, and Mrs. Fairfax answered my advertisement."
-Me anuncié y Mrs. Fairfax contestó a mi anuncio.
"Yes," said the good lady, who now knew what ground we were upon, "and I am daily thankful for the choice Providence led me to make.
-Sí -dijo la buena señora-, y doy gracias al cielo por el acierto que tuve.
Miss Eyre has been an invaluable companion to me, and a kind and careful teacher to Adele."
Miss Eyre ha sido una gran compañera para mí y una bondadosa y útil profesora para Adèle. -No haga el artículo -replicó Mr.
"Don't trouble yourself to give her a character," returned Mr. Rochester: "eulogiums will not bias me; I shall judge for myself.
Los elogios no son mi fuerte. Yo sé juzgar por mí mismo.
She began by felling my horse."
Y lo primero que esta señorita me ha hecho es motivar una caída de mi caballo.
"Sir?" said Mrs. Fairfax.
-¡Oh, señor! -dijo Mrs.
"I have to thank her for this sprain."
Fairfax. -Esta dislocación se la debo a ella.
The widow looked bewildered.
La viuda pareció turbada.
"Miss Eyre, have you ever lived in a town?"
-¿No ha vivido usted nunca en una ciudad, señorita?
"Have you seen much society?" "None but the pupils and teachers of Lowood, and now the inmates of Thornfield."
-¿Ha tratado mucha gente? -Con nadie más que con las condiscípulas y profesores de Lowood y ahora con los habitantes de Thornfield.
"Have you read much?" "Only such books as came in my way; and they have not been numerous or very learned."
-¿Ha leído usted mucho? -Los libros que he encontrado a mi alcance, que no han sido demasiados. -Veo que ha vivido usted como una monja, no cabe duda...
"You have lived the life of a nun: no doubt you are well drilled in religious forms;--Brocklehurst, who I understand directs Lowood, is a parson, is he not?"
Creo que el director de ese colegio es un tal Brocklehurst, un clérigo, ¿no?
"And you girls probably worshipped him, as a convent full of religieuses would worship their director."
-Y supongo que ustedes sentirían hacia su director la estimación de las religiosas de un convento hacia su capellán, ¿no?
"Oh, no."
-No.
"You are very cool! No!
-¿Cómo que no?
What! a novice not worship her priest!
¡Una novicia que no estima a su sacerdote!
That sounds blasphemous."
Eso es casi una impiedad...
"I disliked Mr. Brocklehurst; and I was not alone in the feeling.
-Yo no estimo a Mr. Brocklehurst, ni soy la única que tiene tal opinión.
He is a harsh man; at once pompous and meddling; he cut off our hair; and for economy's sake bought us bad needles and thread, with which we could hardly sew."
Es un hombre duro, mezquino, que hacía que nos cortasen los cabellos y nos escatimaba el hilo y las agujas.
"That was very false economy," remarked Mrs. Fairfax, who now again caught the drift of the dialogue.
-¡Qué modo tan equivocado de entender la economía! -intervino Mrs. Fairfax.
"And was that the head and front of his offending?" demanded Mr. Rochester.
-¿Es ése todo el motivo de disgusto que tiene usted con él? -preguntó Mr. Rochester.

"He starved us when he had the sole superintendence of the provision department, before the committee was appointed; and he bored us with long lectures once a week, and with evening readings from books of his own inditing, about sudden deaths and judgments, which made us afraid to go to bed." "What age were you when you went to Lowood?"

-Nos mataba de hambre cuando estaba a su cargo la organización de las comidas, antes de que se nombrase un patronato. Una vez a la semana nos fatigaba con larguísimas lecturas y todas las noches nos hacía leer libros sobre la muerte repentina y el Juicio Final, que nos hacían acostarnos despavoridas...
"About ten." "And you stayed there eight years: you are now, then, eighteen?"
-¿Qué edad tenía usted cuando ingresó en Lowood? -Diez años. -Entonces, ahora cuenta dieciocho, ¿verdad?
I assented.
Asentí.
"Arithmetic, you see, is useful; without its aid, I should hardly have been able to guess your age.
-La aritmética es útil a veces; sin ella, yo no habría podido ahora adivinar su edad.
It is a point difficult to fix where the features and countenance are so much at variance as in your case.
Es cosa difícil de precisar en ciertos casos...
And now what did you learn at Lowood?
Y ¿qué aprendió usted en Lowood?
Can you play?"
¿Sabe usted tocar?
"Of course: that is the established answer.
-Ya; ésa es la respuesta de rigor.

Go into the library--I mean, if you please.--(Excuse my tone of command; I am used to say, 'Do this,' and it is done: I cannot alter my customary habits for one new inmate.)--Go, then, into the library; take a candle with you; leave the door open; sit down to the piano, and play a tune."
Estoy acostumbrado a decir que se haga esto o lo otro y a ser obedecido, y no voy a violentar mis costumbres por usted. Vaya, pues, a la biblioteca, alúmbrese con una vela y toque una pieza al piano.
I departed, obeying his directions.
Obedecí sus indicaciones.
"Enough!" he called out in a few minutes.
-¡Basta! -gritó al cabo de algunos minutos-.
"You play _a little_, I see; like any other English school-girl; perhaps rather better than some, but not well."
Toca usted un poco, ya lo veo... Como otras muchas chicas de los colegios, y hasta mejor que alguna, pero no bien.
I closed the piano and returned.
Cerré el piano y volví.
Mr. Rochester continued--"Adele showed me some sketches this morning, which she said were yours.
Mr. Rochester continuó: -Adèle me ha enseñado esta mañana unos dibujos de usted, según ella dice.
I don't know whether they were entirely of your doing; probably a master aided you?"
Pero supongo que estarán hechos con la ayuda de algún profesor.
"No, indeed!" I interjected.
-No -me apresuré a decir.
"Ah! that pricks pride.
-Veo que tiene usted cierto orgullo.
Well, fetch me your portfolio, if you can vouch for its contents being original; but don't pass your word unless you are certain: I can recognise patchwork."
Bueno: tráigame su álbum de dibujos y enséñemelos, pero sólo en el caso de que sean auténticamente suyos. A mí no logrará usted engañarme.
"Then I will say nothing, and you shall judge for yourself, sir."
-Entonces no diré nada, para que usted juzgue por sí mismo.
I brought the portfolio from the library.
Fui a buscar el álbum y lo llevé.
Adele and Mrs. Fairfax drew near to see the pictures.
Adèle y Mrs. Fairfax se aproximaron para ver mis dibujos y pinturas.
"No crowding," said Mr. Rochester: "take the drawings from my hand as I finish with them; but don't push your faces up to mine."
Cuando yo concluya, lo cogen ustedes. Entretanto, no se echen encima.
He deliberately scrutinised each sketch and painting. Three he laid aside; the others, when he had examined them, he swept from him.
Examinó cuidadosamente mis trabajos, apartó tres y separó los demás.
"Take them off to the other table, Mrs. Fairfax," said he, "and look at them with Adele;--you" (glancing at me) "resume your seat, and answer my questions.
Fairfax—dijo-, y véanlos usted y Adèle. Y usted -agregó dirigiéndose a mí-, siéntese y conteste a mis preguntas.
I perceive those pictures were done by one hand: was that hand yours?"
Ya veo que estos trabajos son de una misma mano. Esa mano, ¿es la suya?
"And when did you find time to do them?
-¿Cuándo los hizo?
They have taken much time, and some thought."
Deben de haberle costado mucho tiempo.
"I did them in the last two vacations I spent at Lowood, when I had no other occupation."
-Los dibujé en mis dos últimas vacaciones de Lowood. ¡Cómo no tenía nada que hacer!
"Where did you get your copies?" "Out of my head."
-¿De dónde los ha copiado usted? -Los he sacado de mi cabeza.
"That head I see now on your shoulders?"
-¿De esa cabeza que veo sobre sus hombros?
"Has it other furniture of the same kind within?"
-¿Y queda algo parecido dentro de ella?
"I should think it may have: I should hope--better."
-Creo que sí, y hasta pudiera ser que quedase algo mejor.
He spread the pictures before him, and again surveyed them alternately.
El se abstrajo de nuevo en la contemplación de los trabajos.
"Were you happy when you painted these pictures?" asked Mr. Rochester presently.
-¿Se sentía usted feliz cuando los hacía? -dijo al fin.
"I was absorbed, sir: yes, and I was happy.
-Sí, señor.
To paint them, in short, was to enjoy one of the keenest pleasures I have ever known."
El pintar o dibujar ha sido una de las pocas alegrías que yo he tenido en el mundo.
"That is not saying much.
-Eso no es mucho decir.
Your pleasures, by your own account, have been few; but I daresay you did exist in a kind of artist's dreamland while you blent and arranged these strange tints.
Sus placeres, según usted misma afirma, no han sido muy abundantes. Pero se me figura que se extasiaba usted mientras daba a sus pinturas estos extraños matices que emplea.
Did you sit at them long each day?"
¿Trabajaba en ello muchas horas al día?
"I had nothing else to do, because it was the vacation, and I sat at them from morning till noon, and from noon till night: the length of the midsummer days favoured my inclination to apply."
-Como no tenía nada que hacer por estar en vacaciones, trabajaba de sol a sol, y como los días eran largos, disponía de mucho tiempo.
"And you felt self-satisfied with the result of your ardent labours?"
-¿Y está usted satisfecha del resultado de sus esfuerzos
"Far from it.
-No.
I was tormented by the contrast between my idea and my handiwork: in each case I had imagined something which I was quite powerless to realise."
Me atormenta mucho la diferencia que existe entre lo que sueño hacer y lo que hago. Siempre imagino hacer cosas que me resultan imposibles.
"Not quite: you have secured the shadow of your thought; but no more, probably.
-No del todo. Usted ha creado una sombra de lo que soñaba.
You had not enough of the artist's skill and science to give it full being: yet the drawings are, for a school-girl, peculiar. As to the thoughts, they are elfish.
Si no es usted una artista en plena madurez, al menos lo que ha hecho es extraordinario para una escolar.
These eyes in the Evening Star you must have seen in a dream.
Hay detalles que debe de haber visto en sus sueños...
Where did you see Latmos?
Por ejemplo: ¿dónde puede usted, si no, haber visto Patmos?...
For that is Latmos.
Porque esto es Patmos...
There! put the drawings away!"
En fin, llévese todo esto.
I had scarce tied the strings of the portfolio, when, looking at his watch, he said abruptly-- "It is nine o'clock: what are you about, Miss Eyre, to let Adele sit up so long?
Apenas había comenzado a colocar mis trabajos en el álbum, cuando Rochester miró al reloj y dijo bruscamente: -Son las nueve. ¿Cómo está Adèle levantada aún?...
Take her to bed."
Acuéstela, señorita.

Adele went to kiss him before quitting the room: he endured the caress, but scarcely seemed to relish it more than Pilot would have done, nor so much. "I wish you all good-night, now," said he, making a movement of the hand towards the door, in token that he was tired of our company, and wished to dismiss us.

Adèle fue a besarle antes de salir. Él recibió la caricia, pero la correspondió con menos afecto que lo hubiera hecho con el perro. -Buenas noches -nos dijo, señalando la puerta con un ademán, como si, ya cansado de nosotras, nos despidiese.
Mrs. Fairfax folded up her knitting: I took my portfolio: we curtseyed to him, received a frigid bow in return, and so withdrew.
Fairfax recogió su labor, yo mi álbum, nos despedimos de Mr. Rochester, que nos correspondió fríamente, y nos retiramos.
"You said Mr. Rochester was not strikingly peculiar, Mrs. Fairfax," I observed, when I rejoined her in her room, after putting Adele to bed.
Rochester fuera tan especial -dije a Mrs. Fairfax después de que hubimos acostado a la niña.
"Well, is he?"
-¿Y lo es?
"I think so: he is very changeful and abrupt."
-Sí. Es muy brusco y muy voluble.
"True: no doubt he may appear so to a stranger, but I am so accustomed to his manner, I never think of it; and then, if he has peculiarities of temper, allowance should be made." "Why?"
-Sin duda parece algo raro, pero yo estoy acostumbrada a su carácter y nunca pienso en eso. Puesto que tiene un temperamento especial, es preciso seguirle la corriente. -¿Por qué?
"Partly because it is his nature--and we can none of us help our nature; and partly because he has painful thoughts, no doubt, to harass him, and make his spirits unequal."
-En parte, porque su naturaleza sufre y es imposible contrariar la propia naturaleza, y luego porque preocupaciones, penas...
"What about?" "Family troubles, for one thing." "But he has no family."
-¿Acerca de qué? -De disgustos familiares, o cosa parecida. -¿Tiene familia?
"Not now, but he has had--or, at least, relatives.
-Ahora no, pero antes sí.
He lost his elder brother a few years since."
Hace pocos años que murió su hermano mayor.
"His _elder_ brother?"
-¿Su hermano mayor?
"Yes.
-Sí. El actual Mr.
The present Mr. Rochester has not been very long in possession of the property; only about nine years."
Rochester no ha sido siempre dueño de esta propiedad. Sólo hace nueve años que lo es.
"Nine years is a tolerable time. Was he so very fond of his brother as to be still inconsolable for his loss?"
-Yo creo que nueve años es tiempo suficiente para consolarse de la pérdida de un hermano.
"Why, no--perhaps not.
-Quizá no.
I believe there were some misunderstandings between them.
Yo creo que entre ellos hubo disgustos. Mr.
Mr. Rowland Rochester was not quite just to Mr. Edward; and perhaps he prejudiced his father against him.
Rochester no fue justo con Mr. Edward y puede ser que hasta procurase predisponer a su padre contra éste.
The old gentleman was fond of money, and anxious to keep the family estate together.
El padre amaba mucho el dinero y deseaba que las propiedades de la familia estuviesen reunidas en una sola mano.

He did not like to diminish the property by division, and yet he was anxious that Mr. Edward should have wealth, too, to keep up the consequence of the name; and, soon after he was of age, some steps were taken that were not quite fair, and made a great deal of mischief.
No deseaba dividir las tierras y, en consecuencia, Mr. Rowland y su padre realizaron, al parecer, algunas maniobras que dejaban a Mr.

Old Mr. Rochester and Mr. Rowland combined to bring Mr. Edward into what he considered a painful position, for the sake of making his fortune: what the precise nature of that position was I never clearly knew, but his spirit could not brook what he had to suffer in it.
Edward en una situación penosa... No sé exactamente cuál, pero sí sé que era muy desagradable, que produjo no pocos disgustos y que hizo padecer mucho a Mr.
He is not very forgiving: he broke with his family, and now for many years he has led an unsettled kind of life.
Como no es hombre que perdone fácilmente, rompió con su familia y durante muchos años llevó una vida errante.

I don't think he has ever been resident at Thornfield for a fortnight together, since the death of his brother without a will left him master of the estate; and, indeed, no wonder he shuns the old place."
Desde que, por muerte de su hermano, entró en posesión de la herencia, no ha pasado aquí nunca quince días seguidos. No me extraña, en el fondo, que huya de esta casa.
"Why should he shun it?"
-¿Por qué?
"Perhaps he thinks it gloomy." The answer was evasive.
-Porque tiene recuerdos sombríos para él.
I should have liked something clearer; but Mrs. Fairfax either could not, or would not, give me more explicit information of the origin and nature of Mr. Rochester's trials.
Me hubiese agradado pedir algunas explicaciones, pero Mrs. Fairfax no quería o no podía darme detalles más explícitos sobre la naturaleza de las preocupaciones de Mr.
She averred they were a mystery to herself, and that what she knew was chiefly from conjecture.
Acaso fuesen un misterio para ella misma y no supiese sino lo que le permitían imaginar sus conjeturas.
It was evident, indeed, that she wished me to drop the subject, which I did accordingly.
En cualquier caso, como era evidente que deseaba cambiar de conversación, hice por mi parte lo mismo.
For several subsequent days I saw little of Mr. Rochester.
Durante los días siguientes vi pocas veces a Mr. Rochester.
In the mornings he seemed much engaged with business, and, in the afternoon, gentlemen from Millcote or the neighbourhood called, and sometimes stayed to dine with him.
Por las mañanas estaba muy ocupado en sus asuntos y por la tarde le visitaban personas de Millcote o de las cercanías, las cuales, en ocasiones, comían con él.
When his sprain was well enough to admit of horse exercise, he rode out a good deal; probably to return these visits, as he generally did not come back till late at night.
Cuando se repuso de la dislocación, solía salir mucho a caballo, seguramente para devolver aquellas visitas, y no volvía hasta muy entrada la noche.

During this interval, even Adele was seldom sent for to his presence, and all my acquaintance with him was confined to an occasional rencontre in the hall, on the stairs, or in the gallery, when he would sometimes pass me haughtily and coldly, just acknowledging my presence by a distant nod or a cool glance, and sometimes bow and smile with gentlemanlike affability.

En aquel período, aunque Adèle solía ir a verle con frecuencia, todas mis relaciones con él se redujeron a encuentros casuales, en el vestíbulo, la escalera o la galería. En esas ocasiones, él me saludaba con una fría mirada y una distraída inclinación de cabeza, o bien con una sonrisa amable.
His changes of mood did not offend me, because I saw that I had nothing to do with their alternation; the ebb and flow depended on causes quite disconnected with me.
Sus cambios de carácter no me molestaban, ya que era evidente que dependían de causas que para nada se referían a mí.

One day he had had company to dinner, and had sent for my portfolio; in order, doubtless, to exhibit its contents: the gentlemen went away early, to attend a public meeting at Millcote, as Mrs. Fairfax informed me; but the night being wet and inclement, Mr. Rochester did not accompany them.

Un día que estaba comiendo con varios invitados pidió mi álbum, sin duda para que lo viesen. Aquellos caballeros se marcharon pronto, a fin de asistir a una reunión en Millcote, pero él no les acompañó.
Soon after they were gone he rang the bell: a message came that I and Adele were to go downstairs.
A poco de haberse ido sus invitados, tocó la campanilla y ordenó que bajásemos Adèle y yo.

I brushed Adele's hair and made her neat, and having ascertained that I was myself in my usual Quaker trim, where there was nothing to retouch--all being too close and plain, braided locks included, to admit of disarrangement--we descended, Adele wondering whether the _petit coffre_ was at length come; for, owing to some mistake, its arrival had hitherto been delayed.

Yo no tuve que arreglarme, ya que mi vestimenta cuáquera, por lo lisa y rasa, no permitía casi desarreglo alguno. Adèle pensó en seguida si habría llegado su petit coffre que, por no sé qué confusión, sufriera un atraso de varios días.
She was gratified: there it stood, a little carton, on the table when we entered the dining-room. She appeared to know it by instinct.
En cuanto entró en el comedor, vio una cajita de cartón sobre la mesa y se alborozó, como si conociera por instinto de lo que se trataba.
"Ma boite! ma boite!" exclaimed she, running towards it.
-¡Mi caja, mi caja! -exclamó, precipitándose hacia ella.

"Yes, there is your 'boite' at last: take it into a corner, you genuine daughter of Paris, and amuse yourself with disembowelling it," said the deep and rather sarcastic voice of Mr. Rochester, proceeding from the depths of an immense easy-chair at the fireside.
¡Se ve que eres una auténtica parisiense! -dijo la grave y sarcástica voz de Mr. Rochester, surgiendo de las profundidades de una inmensa butaca en que se hallaba hundido, al lado del fuego-.

"And mind," he continued, "don't bother me with any details of the anatomical process, or any notice of the condition of the entrails: let your operation be conducted in silence: tiens-toi tranquille, enfant; comprends-tu?"
Pero no vayas dándonos noticias de tu operación anatómica a medida que investigues en las entrañas de la caja. Hazlo en silencio; tiens-toi tranquille, enfant, comprends-tu?
Adele seemed scarcely to need the warning--she had already retired to a sofa with her treasure, and was busy untying the cord which secured the lid.
Adèle se había retirado a un sofá con su tesoro y se afanaba en soltar la cuerda que lo sujetaba.
Having removed this impediment, and lifted certain silvery envelopes of tissue paper, she merely exclaimed--
Habiendo eliminado tal obstáculo y hallado ciertos objetos envueltos en papel transparente, se limitó a exclamar:
"Oh ciel!
-¡Oh, qué bonito!
Que c'est beau!" and then remained absorbed in ecstatic contemplation.
Y permaneció absorta en una extática contemplación.
"Is Miss Eyre there?" now demanded the master, half rising from his seat to look round to the door, near which I still stood.
-¿Y Miss Eyre? -preguntó el amo, semiincorporándose en su sillón y mirando hacia la puerta, donde yo me hallaba-.
"Ah! well, come forward; be seated here."
Bien, pase y siéntese -continuó, al verme, aproximando una silla a la suya-.
He drew a chair near his own.
No me gusta la charla de los niños.
"I am not fond of the prattle of children," he continued; "for, old bachelor as I am, I have no pleasant associations connected with their lisp.
Soy un solterón y ningún recuerdo grato me producen las cosas infantiles.
It would be intolerable to me to pass a whole evening _tete-a-tete_ with a brat.
Me sería imposible pasar toda la velada téte-à-téte con un chiquillo.
Don't draw that chair farther off, Miss Eyre; sit down exactly where I placed it--if you please, that is.
Digo lo mismo respecto a las viejas, pese a lo que aprecio a la señora Fairfax.
Confound these civilities!
Miss Eyre: siéntese precisamente donde le he señalado...
I continually forget them.
Quiero decir, si gusta...
Nor do I particularly affect simple-minded old ladies.
¡El demonio se lleve esos miramientos tontos! Siempre me olvido de ellos.
He rang, and despatched an invitation to Mrs. Fairfax, who soon arrived, knitting-basket in hand.
Tocó la campanilla y encargó que invitasen a acudir a Mrs. Fairfax, la cual se presentó con su cesto de labor, como de costumbre.
"Good evening, madam; I sent to you for a charitable purpose.
-Buenas noches, señora. He prohibido a Adèle que me hable a propósito de los regalos.

I have forbidden Adele to talk to me about her presents, and she is bursting with repletion: have the goodness to serve her as auditress and interlocutrice; it will be one of the most benevolent acts you ever performed."
Le ruego que me sustituya en la tarea de atenderla y de conversar sobre ese tema. Con ello hará usted una obra de caridad.

Adele, indeed, no sooner saw Mrs. Fairfax, than she summoned her to her sofa, and there quickly filled her lap with the porcelain, the ivory, the waxen contents of her "boite;" pouring out, meantime, explanations and raptures in such broken English as she was mistress of.

Adèle en efecto, apenas vio al ama de llaves, la condujo al sofá en seguida y colmó su falda con las porcelanas y marfiles de que estaban hechos los regalos, entregándose a explicaciones y arrebatos de júbilo tan vehementes como se lo permitía su escaso dominio del inglés.
"Now I have performed the part of a good host," pursued Mr. Rochester, "put my guests into the way of amusing each other, I ought to be at liberty to attend to my own pleasure.
-Ya he cumplido mis deberes de anfitrión dando a mis huéspedes ocasión de divertirse el uno al otro -dijo Rochester- y quedo, pues, en libertad de divertirme yo.
Miss Eyre, draw your chair still a little farther forward: you are yet too far back; I cannot see you without disturbing my position in this comfortable chair, which I have no mind to do."
Señorita: haga el favor de aproximarse más al fuego. Desde aquí no puedo verla sin abandonar la cómoda posición en que estoy sentado, y no tengo ganas de hacer tal cosa.
I did as I was bid, though I would much rather have remained somewhat in the shade; but Mr. Rochester had such a direct way of giving orders, it seemed a matter of course to obey him promptly.
Pero Mr. Rochester tenía un modo de dar órdenes que obligaba a obedecerle sin discusión posible.

We were, as I have said, in the dining-room: the lustre, which had been lit for dinner, filled the room with a festal breadth of light; the large fire was all red and clear; the purple curtains hung rich and ample before the lofty window and loftier arch; everything was still, save the subdued chat of Adele (she dared not speak loud), and, filling up each pause, the beating of winter rain against the panes.

El rojo fuego ardía alegremente y los cortinajes de púrpura pendían, ricos y amplios, de los altos ventanales y el elevado arco de acceso. Todo estaba en silencio, y sólo se oían el cuchicheo de Adèle, que no se atrevía a hablar alto, y el batir de la lluvia invernal en los cristales.
Mr. Rochester, as he sat in his damask-covered chair, looked different to what I had seen him look before; not quite so stern--much less gloomy.
Mr. Rochester, que estaba sentado en su butaca forrada de damasco, miraba de un modo inusitado en él, con menos dureza que de costumbre y de modo mucho menos sombrío.
There was a smile on his lips, and his eyes sparkled, whether with wine or not, I am not sure; but I think it very probable.
Por sus labios vagaba una sonrisa y sus ojos brillaban, ignoro si como consecuencia de haber bebido mucho, aunque me parece probable que sí.

He was, in short, in his after-dinner mood; more expanded and genial, and also more self- indulgent than the frigid and rigid temper of the morning; still he looked preciously grim, cushioning his massive head against the swelling back of his chair, and receiving the light of the fire on his granite- hewn features, and in his great, dark eyes; for he had great, dark eyes, and very fine eyes, too--not without a certain change in their depths sometimes, which, if it was not softness, reminded you, at least, of that feeling.

Estaba, en resumen, en el momento beatífico de la digestión, y se sentía más expansivo y más indulgente que por la mañana. Reclinaba su maciza cabeza sobre el blanco respaldo del sillón, la lumbre iluminaba de lleno sus duras facciones y en sus ojos, grandes y negros, muy bellos por cierto, había algo que si no era dulzura podía considerarse como una manifestación parecida a ese sentimiento.
He had been looking two minutes at the fire, and I had been looking the same length of time at him, when, turning suddenly, he caught my gaze fastened on his physiognomy.
Miró el fuego durante algunos instantes, volvió la cabeza de pronto y me sorprendió examinando su fisonomía.
"You examine me, Miss Eyre," said he: "do you think me handsome?"
-Me contempla usted -dijo-. ¿Le parezco guapo?
I should, if I had deliberated, have replied to this question by something conventionally vague and polite; but the answer somehow slipped from my tongue before I was aware
De haberlo meditado, yo hubiese dado una contestación cortés, pero la respuesta brotó de mis labios antes de que tuviese tiempo de reflexionar:
--"No, sir."
-No, señor.

"Ah! By my word! there is something singular about you," said he: "you have the air of a little _nonnette_; quaint, quiet, grave, and simple, as you sit with your hands before you, and your eyes generally bent on the carpet (except, by-the-bye, when they are directed piercingly to my face; as just now, for instance); and when one asks you a question, or makes a remark to which you are obliged to reply, you rap out a round rejoinder, which, if not blunt, is at least brusque.

-Palabra que es usted rara de veras -dijo-. Está usted quieta, grave y silenciosa como una monjita, con las manos cruzadas y mirando la alfombra (excepto cuando, como ahora, me mira a la cara) y, en cambio, si se le hace alguna pregunta, sale con una contestación si no grosera, al menos brusca.
What do you mean by it?"
¿Qué significa eso?
"Sir, I was too plain; I beg your pardon.
-Perdóneme, señor.

I ought to have replied that it was not easy to give an impromptu answer to a question about appearances; that tastes mostly differ; and that beauty is of little consequence, or something of that sort."
Reconozco que yo debía contestar que no es fácil responder a tal pregunta guiándose por las apariencias; que eso va en gustos; que la hermosura en los hombres tiene poca importancia, o algo parecido.
Beauty of little consequence, indeed!
-¿Cómo que no tiene importancia la hermosura?
And so, under pretence of softening the previous outrage, of stroking and soothing me into placidity, you stick a sly penknife under my ear!
Ahora, so pretexto de paliar el insulto anterior, me introduce, tranquilamente, un cuchillo afilado en el oído. ¡Porque no otra cosa son sus palabras!
Go on: what fault do you find with me, pray?
Dígame: ¿qué defectos encuentra en mí?
I suppose I have all my limbs and all my features like any other man?"
¿Acaso no tengo mis miembros y mis facciones completos, como los demás hombres?
"Mr. Rochester, allow me to disown my first answer: I intended no pointed repartee: it was only a blunder."
-He querido rectificar mi contestación, señor. Era un disparate.
"Just so: I think so: and you shall be answerable for it.
-Lo mismo creo. Ea, critique mi figura.
Criticise me: does my forehead not please you?"
¿Acaso no le gusta mi frente?

He lifted up the sable waves of hair which lay horizontally over his brow, and showed a solid enough mass of intellectual organs, but an abrupt deficiency where the suave sign of benevolence should have risen.
Separó los cabellos que caían sobre sus cejas y mostró una sólida envoltura de los órganos intelectuales, en la que las protuberancias características de la bondad brillaban por su ausencia.
"Now, ma'am, am I a fool?"
-¿Qué? ¿Acaso tengo aspecto de tonto?
"Far from it, sir.
-Nada de eso, señor.
You would, perhaps, think me rude if I inquired in return whether you are a philanthropist?"
¿Me encontrará usted grosera si le pregunto, a mi vez, si tiene usted algo de filántropo?
"There again! Another stick of the penknife, when she pretended to pat my head: and that is because I said I did not like the society of children and old women (low be it spoken!).
-¡Ea, otra cuchilla, con la disculpa de acariciarme! ¡Y todo porque he dicho que no me gusta tratar con los niños y las viejas!

No, young lady, I am not a general philanthropist; but I bear a conscience;" and he pointed to the prominences which are said to indicate that faculty, and which, fortunately for him, were sufficiently conspicuous; giving, indeed, a marked breadth to the upper part of his head: "and, besides, I once had a kind of rude tenderness of heart.

No, jovencita, no soy un filántropo, pero tengo conciencia. Y señaló las prominencias que, según se dice, indican tal cualidad y que, afortunadamente para él, eran bastante acusadas. -Además -agregó-, poseo una especie de ruda blandura de corazón.

When I was as old as you, I was a feeling fellow enough, partial to the unfledged, unfostered, and unlucky; but Fortune has knocked me about since: she has even kneaded me with her knuckles, and now I flatter myself I am hard and tough as an India-rubber ball; pervious, though, through a chink or two still, and with one sentient point in the middle of the lump.

Cuando yo tenía la edad de usted, era un muchacho bastante sentimental y me emocionaba fácilmente ante los infortunados y los desvalidos. Pero después la fortuna me ha baquetado de tal modo, que me he hecho duro y resistente como una pelota de goma maciza.
Yes: does that leave hope for me?"
No obstante, soy vulnerable por una o dos hendiduras, tengo algún punto flaco... ¿Me concede eso alguna esperanza?
"Hope of what, sir?"
-¿De qué, señor?
"Of my final re-transformation from India-rubber back to flesh?"
-De volver a transformarme, de pelota de goma maciza que soy, en un ser de carne y hueso.
"Decidedly he has had too much wine," I thought; and I did not know what answer to make to his queer question: how could I tell whether he was capable of being re-transformed?
Y no supe qué contestar. ¿Qué podía decirle sobre sus posibilidades de transformación?

"You looked very much puzzled, Miss Eyre; and though you are not pretty any more than I am handsome, yet a puzzled air becomes you; besides, it is convenient, for it keeps those searching eyes of yours away from my physiognomy, and busies them with the worsted flowers of the rug; so puzzle on.
-Me mira usted con asombro, señorita, y como usted no tiene mucho más de bonita que yo de guapo, el asombro no la favorece en nada, se lo aseguro.
Young lady, I am disposed to be gregarious and communicative to-night."
Le conviene escucharme, porque así separará sus ojos de mi cara y se dedicará a estudiar las flores de la alfombra. Jovencita: esta noche me siento comunicativo y sociable.

With this announcement he rose from his chair, and stood, leaning his arm on the marble mantelpiece: in that attitude his shape was seen plainly as well as his face; his unusual breadth of chest, disproportionate almost to his length of limb.
En tal actitud, se le veía el cuerpo tan bien como la cara. Su pecho tenía un perímetro casi desproporcionado a la longitud de sus brazos y piernas.

I am sure most people would have thought him an ugly man; yet there was so much unconscious pride in his port; so much ease in his demeanour; such a look of complete indifference to his own external appearance; so haughty a reliance on the power of other qualities, intrinsic or adventitious, to atone for the lack of mere personal attractiveness, that, in looking at him, one inevitably shared the indifference, and, even in a blind, imperfect sense, put faith in the confidence.

Estoy segura de que la gente le hubiera juzgado un hombre muy desagradable; pero, sin embargo, había tan espontánea altivez en su porte, tanta naturalidad en sus modales, tan sincera indiferencia hacia la fealdad de su exterior, tan firme creencia en la importancia de otras facultades suyas -intrínsecas o no, pero al margen del mero atractivo personal-, que, al mirarle, la indiferencia desaparecía y se sentía uno inclinado a confiar en él.

"I am disposed to be gregarious and communicative to-night," he repeated, "and that is why I sent for you: the fire and the chandelier were not sufficient company for me; nor would Pilot have been, for none of these can talk.

-Repito que esta noche me siento comunicativo y sociable -siguió-, y por eso he enviado a buscarla, ya que el fuego y los candelabros no me parecieron suficiente compañía; ni tampoco Piloto, ya que, como todos sus congéneres, no habla.
Adele is a degree better, but still far below the mark; Mrs. Fairfax ditto; you, I am persuaded, can suit me if you will: you puzzled me the first evening I invited you down here.
Fairfax, ídem. En cambio, estoy persuadido de que usted se pondrá a mi altura, si se lo propone.
I have almost forgotten you since: other ideas have driven yours from my head; but to-night I am resolved to be at ease; to dismiss what importunes, and recall what pleases.
Me dejó usted confundido la primera noche que la invité, luego la olvidé casi del todo. Tenía otras ideas en la cabeza.
It would please me now to draw you out--to learn more of you--therefore speak."
Esta noche he resuelto estar a mis anchas, despidiendo a los importunos y llamando a los que me complacen. Me agradará saber más cosas de usted.
Instead of speaking, I smiled; and not a very complacent or submissive smile either.
En vez de hablar, sonreí, y creo que no de un modo muy complaciente ni sumiso.
"Speak," he urged.
-Hable -insistió.
"What about, sir?" "Whatever you like.
-¿De qué?
I leave both the choice of subject and the manner of treating it entirely to yourself."
-De lo que quiera. Dejo a su elección el tema y la forma de desarrollarlo, siempre que se refiera a usted misma.
Accordingly I sat and said nothing: "If he expects me to talk for the mere sake of talking and showing off, he will find he has addressed himself to the wrong person," I thought.
Yo no dije nada.
"You are dumb, Miss Eyre."
-¿Está usted muda, señorita?
I was dumb still.
Continué callada.
He bent his head a little towards me, and with a single hasty glance seemed to dive into my eyes.
Él inclinó la cabeza hacia mí y me miró de un modo singular.
"Stubborn?" he said, "and annoyed.
-¿Conque se ha enojado usted? -dijo-.
Ah! it is consistent.
Comprendo.
I put my request in an absurd, almost insolent form.
Me he dirigido a usted en una forma absurda y casi insolente.
Miss Eyre, I beg your pardon.
Perdone.

The fact is, once for all, I don't wish to treat you like an inferior: that is" (correcting himself), "I claim only such superiority as must result from twenty years' difference in age and a century's advance in experience.

Conste, de una vez para siempre, que no quiero tratarla como a un inferior..., es decir -corrigió en seguida-, únicamente con la superioridad que me dan veinte años más de edad y cien años más de experiencia.

This is legitimate, _et j'y tiens_, as Adele would say; and it is by virtue of this superiority, and this alone, that I desire you to have the goodness to talk to me a little now, and divert my thoughts, which are galled with dwelling on one point--cankering as a rusty nail."
Esto es natural, tenez, como diría Adèle. Sólo en virtud de esa superioridad he rogado a usted que tenga la bondad de hablarme un poco, para distraerme de otra clase de pensamientos.
He had deigned an explanation, almost an apology, and I did not feel insensible to his condescension, and would not seem so.
Se había dignado darme una explicación, casi una excusa. No cabía mostrarse insensible a su condescendencia.
"I am willing to amuse you, if I can, sir--quite willing; but I cannot introduce a topic, because how do I know what will interest you?
-Me agradaría distraerle, si pudiera, señor, pero no sé de qué hablar, porque, ¿cómo adivinar lo que le interesa?
Ask me questions, and I will do my best to answer them."
Pregúnteme lo que quiera y le contestaré lo mejor que sepa.

"Then, in the first place, do you agree with me that I have a right to be a little masterful, abrupt, perhaps exacting, sometimes, on the grounds I stated, namely, that I am old enough to be your father, and that I have battled through a varied experience with many men of many nations, and roamed over half the globe, while you have lived quietly with one set of people in one house?"

-Entonces, hágame el favor de concordar conmigo en que me asiste el derecho de hablarle con cierta autoridad, teniendo en cuenta que por la edad podría ser su padre, además de que poseo una larga experiencia, adquirida viajando por medio mundo y tratando a muchas y diversas gentes, mientras usted ha vivido siempre con las mismas en la misma casa.
"Do as you please, sir."
-Como usted guste, señor.
"That is no answer; or rather it is a very irritating, because a very evasive one.
-Eso es una desagradable evasiva.
Reply clearly."
Conteste con claridad.

"I don't think, sir, you have a right to command me, merely because you are older than I, or because you have seen more of the world than I have; your claim to superiority depends on the use you have made of your time and experience."

-Pues bien, señor, yo creo que usted no tiene derecho a mandarme porque sea más viejo que yo o porque haya visto más mundo. Esa superioridad que usted se atribuye dependerá del uso que haya hecho de su tiempo y de su experiencia.
"Humph!
-¡Hum!
Promptly spoken. But I won't allow that, seeing that it would never suit my case, as I have made an indifferent, not to say a bad, use of both advantages.
Creo que he hecho un uso indiferente, por no decir malo, de esas dos ventajas a mi favor.
Leaving superiority out of the question, then, you must still agree to receive my orders now and then, without being piqued or hurt by the tone of command. Will you?"
Bien: dejemos al margen esa superioridad y pongámonos de acuerdo en que usted no se ofenderá si recibe órdenes mías ahora o en adelante, ¿le parece bien?
I smiled: I thought to myself Mr. Rochester _is_ peculiar--he seems to forget that he pays me 30 pounds per annum for receiving his orders.
Sonreí al pensar en lo curioso de que Mr. Rochester, al hablar de órdenes, olvidase que me pagaba treinta libras al año para tener el derecho de dármelas.
"The smile is very well," said he, catching instantly the passing expression; "but speak too."
-¡Elocuente sonrisa, señorita!- dijo él, sorpendiéndola y comprendiendo mi pensamiento.
"I was thinking, sir, that very few masters would trouble themselves to inquire whether or not their paid subordinates were piqued and hurt by their orders."
-Estaba pensando, señor, que pocas personas se preocuparían de preguntar a sus asalariados si les ofendían o no las órdenes que les dieran.
"Paid subordinates!
-¿Asalariados?
What! you are my paid subordinate, are you?
¿Es usted asalariada mía?
Oh yes, I had forgotten the salary! Well then, on that mercenary ground, will you agree to let me hector a little?"
¡Ah, sí: me había olvidado del sueldo!
"No, sir, not on that ground; but, on the ground that you did forget it, and that you care whether or not a dependent is comfortable in his dependency, I agree heartily."
Bueno, puestos en ese terreno mercenario, ¿está usted de acuerdo en dejarme adoptar un poquito el aire de hombre superior?
"And will you consent to dispense with a great many conventional forms and phrases, without thinking that the omission arises from insolence?"
¿Consiente en dispensarme muchas faltas a las formas y a las frases convencionales, sin suponer que la omisión entraña insolencia?
"I am sure, sir, I should never mistake informality for insolence: one I rather like, the other nothing free-born would submit to, even for a salary."

-Estoy segura, señor, de que nunca confundiré la falta de buenas formas con la insolencia. Lo primero me parece bien; a lo segundo, ningún ser humano nacido libre debe someterse, ni siquiera por un sueldo.
"Humbug!
-¡Bobadas!
Most things free-born will submit to anything for a salary; therefore, keep to yourself, and don't venture on generalities of which you are intensely ignorant.
La mayoría de los nacidos libres se someten por un sueldo. Refiérase a sí misma y no entre en generalizaciones que usted ignora en absoluto.

However, I mentally shake hands with you for your answer, despite its inaccuracy; and as much for the manner in which it was said, as for the substance of the speech; the manner was frank and sincere; one does not often see such a manner: no, on the contrary, affectation, or coldness, or stupid, coarse-minded misapprehension of one's meaning are the usual rewards of candour.
No obstante, mentalmente coincido con su contestación, a pesar de su inexactitud, tanto por el modo de decirlo como por la idea que entraña. El modo ha sido franco y sincero, cosa poco corriente.
Not three in three thousand raw school-girl-governesses would have answered me as you have just done.
Ni tres entre tres mil institutrices hubieran contestado como usted lo ha hecho.
But I don't mean to flatter you: if you are cast in a different mould to the majority, it is no merit of yours: Nature did it.
Pero no se vanaglorie de ello. Si es usted diferente a la mayoría, se lo debe a la naturaleza, que la ha hecho así.
And then, after all, I go too fast in my conclusions: for what I yet know, you may be no better than the rest; you may have intolerable defects to counterbalance your few good points."
Y aún creo que voy demasiado lejos en mi criterio, porque acaso no sea usted mejor que las demás y tenga intolerables defectos que compensen sus buenas cualidades.
"And so may you," I thought.
«Lo mismo puede pasarte a ti», pensé.
My eye met his as the idea crossed my mind: he seemed to read the glance, answering as if its import had been spoken as well as imagined--
Él debió de leer en mis ojos aquel pensamiento, porque me contestó como si me lo hubiera oído exponer de palabra:
"Yes, yes, you are right," said he; "I have plenty of faults of my own: I know it, and I don't wish to palliate them, I assure you.
Tiene usted razón. Yo estoy cargado de defectos.

God wot I need not be too severe about others; I have a past existence, a series of deeds, a colour of life to contemplate within my own breast, which might well call my sneers and censures from my neighbours to myself.
Lo sé, y no trato de negarlos, se lo aseguro. No puedo ser muy severo con los demás, porque mi propia vida ha sido tal, que con justicia merece las censuras, del prójimo.

I started, or rather (for like other defaulters, I like to lay half the blame on ill fortune and adverse circumstances) was thrust on to a wrong tack at the age of one-and-twenty, and have never recovered the right course since: but I might have been very different; I might have been as good as you--wiser--almost as stainless.

Yo inicié o, mejor dicho, me hicieron iniciar (a mí, como a todos los equivocados, nos gusta achacar la mitad de nuestra mala suerte a las circunstancias adversas) un camino tortuoso cuando sólo tenía veinte años, y luego no he podido seguir el recto. Pero yo habría podido ser muy diferente, tan bueno como usted, casi tan puro y, desde luego, más sensato.
I envy you your peace of mind, your clean conscience, your unpolluted memory.
Envidio su tranquilidad mental, su conciencia limpia, su memoria libre de todo recuerdo ominoso.
Little girl, a memory without blot or contamination must be an exquisite treasure--an inexhaustible source of pure refreshment: is it not?"
Una conciencia así, joven, es un exquisito tesoro, un manantial inagotable de confortaciones...
"How was your memory when you were eighteen, sir?"
-¿Cómo era su conciencia a los dieciocho años, señor?
"All right then; limpid, salubrious: no gush of bilge water had turned it to fetid puddle.
-Como la de usted: limpia y clara, sin que una sola gota de agua turbia la hubiese contaminado aún.
I was your equal at eighteen--quite your equal.
Yo era como usted, igual que usted.
Nature meant me to be, on the whole, a good man, Miss Eyre; one of the better kind, and you see I am not so.
La naturaleza, señorita, me inclinaba a ser un hombre bueno, y ya ve usted que no lo soy.
You would say you don't see it; at least I flatter myself I read as much in your eye (beware, by-the-bye, what you express with that organ; I am quick at interpreting its language).
Está usted pensando que me adulo a mí mismo: lo leo en sus ojos, y yo comprendo enseguida ese lenguaje...

Then take my word for it,--I am not a villain: you are not to suppose that--not to attribute to me any such bad eminence; but, owing, I verily believe, rather to circumstances than to my natural bent, I am a trite commonplace sinner, hackneyed in all the poor petty dissipations with which the rich and worthless try to put on life.

Pero le doy mi palabra de que digo la verdad, y supongo que no me tendrá usted por un villano... Yo he dado, más que por natural inclinación, en virtud de las circunstancias, en ser un pecador como hay muchos, encenagado en todas las miserables disipaciones que envilecen la vida.
Do you wonder that I avow this to you?
No le extrañe.

Know, that in the course of your future life you will often find yourself elected the involuntary confidant of your acquaintances' secrets: people will instinctively find out, as I have done, that it is not your forte to tell of yourself, but to listen while others talk of themselves; they will feel, too, that you listen with no malevolent scorn of their indiscretion, but with a kind of innate sympathy; not the less comforting and encouraging because it is very unobtrusive in its manifestations."

En el curso de su vida encontrará usted mucha gente que le confía sus secretos, involuntariamente, de un modo instintivo, y ello, porque usted prefiere, a hablar de sí misma, oír hablar de sí mismos a los demás, escuchándoles con una natural simpatía, que es más agradable y anima más porque no es inoportuna en sus manifestaciones.
"How do you know?--how can you guess all this, sir?"
-¿Cómo lo adivina usted, señor? -Lo veo con toda evidencia.
"I know it well; therefore I proceed almost as freely as if I were writing my thoughts in a diary.
Y la estoy hablando tan sinceramente como si escribiese mis pensamientos en un diario íntimo.
You would say, I should have been superior to circumstances; so I should--so I should; but you see I was not.
Respecto de mi vida, podría usted decir que yo debiera haber procurado superar las circunstancias, pero la verdad es que no lo hice.
When fate wronged me, I had not the wisdom to remain cool: I turned desperate; then I degenerated.
En vez de recibir con impasibilidad los golpes del destino, me dejé caer en la depravación...
Now, when any vicious simpleton excites my disgust by his paltry ribaldry, I cannot flatter myself that I am better than he: I am forced to confess that he and I are on a level.
Y he aquí que ahora, cuando el ver un degenerado cualquiera excita mi repulsión, no puedo considerarme mejor que él...
Dread remorse when you are tempted to err, Miss Eyre; remorse is the poison of life."
En fin, señorita, cuando uno cae en el error siente luego remordimientos y, créalo, el remordimiento es el veneno de la vida.
"Repentance is said to be its cure, sir."
-Pero el arrepentimiento es el antídoto de ese veneno, señor.
"It is not its cure. Reformation may be its cure; and I could reform--I have strength yet for that--if--but where is the use of thinking of it, hampered, burdened, cursed as I am?
-No lo es; el cambiar de conducta, sí; y acaso yo cambiara en el caso de... Pero ¿a qué hablar de lo que es imposible?
Besides, since happiness is irrevocably denied me, I have a right to get pleasure out of life: and I _will_ get it, cost what it may."
Además, puesto que se me niega la felicidad, tengo derecho a gozar de los placeres que pueda encontrar en la vida; y así lo haré, cueste lo que cueste.
"Then you will degenerate still more, sir."
-Y se depravará cada vez más, señor.
"Possibly: yet why should I, if I can get sweet, fresh pleasure? And I may get it as sweet and fresh as the wild honey the bee gathers on the moor."
-Puede ser. O acaso no, porque, ¿y si encuentro en esos placeres algo confortable y dulce, tan confortable y dulce como la miel silvestre que la abeja acumula entre los brezales?
"It will sting--it will taste bitter, sir."
¡Qué amargo debe de ser eso!
"How do you know?--you never tried it.
-¿Qué sabe usted?
How very serious--how very solemn you look: and you are as ignorant of the matter as this cameo head" (taking one from the mantelpiece).
Por muy seria que se ponga y por muy solemnemente que me mire, está usted tan ignorante del asunto como este camafeo lo pueda estar -y tomó uno de la chimenea-.

"You have no right to preach to me, you neophyte, that have not passed the porch of life, and are absolutely unacquainted with its mysteries." "I only remind you of your own words, sir: you said error brought remorse, and you pronounced remorse the poison of existence."

No tiene usted derecho á sermonearme; es usted una neófita que no ha pasado aún bajo el pórtico de la vida y desconoce sus misterios. -Me limito a recordarle, señor, que, según usted mismo, el error apareja remordimiento y el remordimiento es el veneno de la existencia.
"And who talks of error now?
-¿Quién habla de error ahora?
I scarcely think the notion that flittered across my brain was an error. I believe it was an inspiration rather than a temptation: it was very genial, very soothing--I know that.
¿Quién puede decir si la idea que acude a la mente es un error o más bien una inspiración?
Here it comes again!
¡Ahora mismo siento una idea que me tienta!
It is no devil, I assure you; or if it be, it has put on the robes of an angel of light.
Y le aseguro que no es nada diabólica. Al menos, se presenta engalanada con las vestiduras luminosas de un ángel.
I think I must admit so fair a guest when it asks entrance to my heart."
¿Cómo no admitir a un visitante que se introduce en el alma tan radiante de luz?
"Distrust it, sir; it is not a true angel."
-No es un ángel verdadero, señor.
"Once more, how do you know?
-¿Qué sabe usted, repito?
By what instinct do you pretend to distinguish between a fallen seraph of the abyss and a messenger from the eternal throne--between a guide and a seducer?"
¿En virtud de qué pretende usted distinguir entre un ángel caído y un emisario celestial?
"I judged by your countenance, sir, which was troubled when you said the suggestion had returned upon you. I feel sure it will work you more misery if you listen to it."
-Lo juzgo por su aspecto, señor. Estoy segura de que será usted muy desgraciado si atiende la sugestión que debe de haber recibido en este momento.
"Not at all--it bears the most gracious message in the world: for the rest, you are not my conscience-keeper, so don't make yourself uneasy.
Al menos, me trae el más agradable mensaje que pueda pedirse. Además, ¿es acaso usted mi directora espiritual?
Here, come in, bonny wanderer!"
¡Ea, linda aparición, ven aquí!
He said this as if he spoke to a vision, viewless to any eye but his own; then, folding his arms, which he had half extended, on his chest, he seemed to enclose in their embrace the invisible being.
Hablaba como si se dirigiese a una visión, no distinguible a otros ojos que los suyos. Abrió los brazos y luego los cerró sobre su pecho, como si abrazase a alguien.
"Now," he continued, again addressing me, "I have received the pilgrim--a disguised deity, as I verily believe.
-Ahora -continuó, dirigiéndose a mí-, ya he recibido al bello peregrino, a la deidad disfrazada, como lo es sin duda.
Already it has done me good: my heart was a sort of charnel; it will now be a shrine."
Su aparición me ha causado un efecto benéfico: mi corazón, que era un osario hace un momento, es casi un sagrario en este instante.
"To speak truth, sir, I don't understand you at all: I cannot keep up the conversation, because it has got out of my depth.
-A decir verdad, señor, no puedo seguirle en su conversación. No la comprendo; queda fuera de mi alcance.

Only one thing, I know: you said you were not as good as you should like to be, and that you regretted your own imperfection;--one thing I can comprehend: you intimated that to have a sullied memory was a perpetual bane.
Sólo creo entender una cosa: que no es usted tan bueno como quisiera, y que lamenta su imperfección. Antes me hablaba usted de memoria.

It seems to me, that if you tried hard, you would in time find it possible to become what you yourself would approve; and that if from this day you began with resolution to correct your thoughts and actions, you would in a few years have laid up a new and stainless store of recollections, to which you might revert with pleasure."

Pues bien, yo estoy convencida de que, si usted se lo propusiera, llegaría a corregir sus pensamientos y sus actos hasta que llegase el día en que, al repasar sus recuerdos, los hallase agradables en vez de dolorosos.
"Justly thought; rightly said, Miss Eyre; and, at this moment, I am paving hell with energy."
-Bien pensando y mejor dicho, señorita.
"I am laying down good intentions, which I believe durable as flint.
En este momento procuro con todas mis fuerzas adquirir nuevos y buenos propósitos, que habrán de ser tan firmes y duraderos como la misma roca.
Certainly, my associates and pursuits shall be other than they have been."
Desde ahora creo que mis pensamientos y mis deseos van a ser muy distintos a los de antes.
"And better?"
-¿Y mejores?
"And better--so much better as pure ore is than foul dross.
-Tanto como el oro puro es mejor que el metal dorado.
You seem to doubt me; I don't doubt myself: I know what my aim is, what my motives are; and at this moment I pass a law, unalterable as that of the Medes and Persians, that both are right."
Parece que duda usted, pero yo no dudo de mí mismo. Conozco mi fin y los motivos que tengo para buscarlo, y desde este instante me someto a una ley tan inflexible como la de los persas y los medos.
"They cannot be, sir, if they require a new statute to legalise them."
-No lo conseguirá, señor, si no establece a la vez reglas para aplicarla.
"They are, Miss Eyre, though they absolutely require a new statute: unheard-of combinations of circumstances demand unheard-of rules."
-Pero esas reglas han de ser inusitadas, porque es una inusitada concurrencia de circunstancias la que las impone.
"That sounds a dangerous maxim, sir; because one can see at once that it is liable to abuse."
-Semejante máxima es peligrosa, porque se presta a interpretaciones torcidas.
"Sententious sage! so it is: but I swear by my household gods not to abuse it."
-¡Qué sentenciosa está usted hoy! Pero le aseguro que no interpretaré torcidamente nada.
"You are human and fallible."
-Usted, como hombre, es falible. -Ya lo sé.
"I am: so are you--what then?"
También usted lo es. ¿Y qué?
"The human and fallible should not arrogate a power with which the divine and perfect alone can be safely intrusted."
-Que quien es falible no puede arrogarse el poder de seguir una línea de conducta extraordinaria asegurando que es conveniente.
"'Let it be right'--the very words: you have pronounced them."
-¡«Que es conveniente»! Ésa es la frase adecuada.

"_May_ it be right then," I said, as I rose, deeming it useless to continue a discourse which was all darkness to me; and, besides, sensible that the character of my interlocutor was beyond my penetration; at least, beyond its present reach; and feeling the uncertainty, the vague sense of insecurity, which accompanies a conviction of ignorance.

Me levanté, comprendiendo lo vano de continuar una conversación de la que no comprendía nada, e intuyendo, además, que el carácter de mi interlocutor era superior a mi penetración. Me sentía indecisa y vacilante, como siempre que se trata de un tema que se ignora.
"Where are you going?"
-¿Adónde va? -A acostar a Adèle.
"To put Adele to bed: it is past her bedtime."
Ya es hora.
"You are afraid of me, because I talk like a Sphynx."
-Me teme usted, porque hablo como la Esfinge.
"Your language is enigmatical, sir: but though I am bewildered, I am certainly not afraid."
